lead: A learning program needs examples. When each example carries the answer we want — a rupee amount, a yes/no, a class name — the program can learn a map from input to answer. That is supervised learning. When the examples carry no answer, the program can still find groups or a shorter description of the data; that is unsupervised learning. Almost every practical system begins in one of these two settings: face unlock, UPI fraud flags, product grouping on a shopping app.
prereq: You need: 1.1, which defines machine learning as fitting rules from data instead of writing them by hand.

blocks.text: A dataset is a table. Each row is one example, say one customer. Each column, except the answer column, is a feature: a number we measured, such as monthly spend in rupees. Call the feature vector x.

If the table also has an answer column — the label y — the task is supervised. If we delete that column and keep only the x columns, the very same rows can be studied unsupervised. The data has not changed. What changed is whether an answer was given to us.

With the label you can ask: given a new spend, is this customer a high spender? Without it you can only ask: which spends naturally sit together? The second answer is a description, not a prediction of a named class.
Supervised learning gets N examples, each a pair (xᵢ, yᵢ). The model is a function f with parameters θ, its weights. Training searches for the θ that makes f(xᵢ; θ) close to yᵢ on every training row.
θ* = argmin over θ of  (1/N) Σᵢ L( f(xᵢ; θ), yᵢ )
blocks.where: θ* is the best parameter setting; N is the number of labelled rows; xᵢ is the feature vector of row i; yᵢ is its label; f(xᵢ; θ) is the model output for that row; L is the loss, small when the output matches the label; argmin picks the θ giving the smallest value.

blocks.text: The kind of y splits supervised learning in two. If y is a class from a fixed list — spam or not spam, digit 0 to 9 — the task is classification. If y is a real quantity — tomorrow's temperature in °C, a house price in rupees — the task is regression. The output layer and the loss must match: cross-entropy for classes, squared error for numbers (see 1.8).

items: Classification: y takes one of K fixed classes. Accuracy is the usual score.
Regression: y is a real number. Mean absolute or mean squared error is the usual score.
The search for the minimum is backpropagation (1.9) plus an optimiser (Unit 2).

blocks.text: Unsupervised learning gets only the x rows. There is no y, so no fixed right answer exists to compare against. The goal must be invented. Most invented goals are one of two kinds.

items: Clustering: put rows into groups so rows in a group are close to each other and far from other groups. k-means is the standard example.
Dimensionality reduction: replace many columns with a few new ones that keep most of the variation, so the data can be plotted or stored cheaply.

blocks.text: "Close" needs a number. For two feature vectors a and b with D features, the Euclidean distance is:
d(a, b) = √( Σⱼ (aⱼ − bⱼ)² ),  j = 1 … D
blocks.where: aⱼ and bⱼ are feature j of the two rows; D is the number of features; d is a distance in the same units as the features, here rupees.

blocks.text: k-means alternates two steps: assign each row to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of the rows assigned to it. Repeat until the centres stop moving. The answer depends on the starting centres, so two runs can number the same group differently.

sections.h3: Where the other two settings sit

blocks.text: Semi-supervised learning has a few labelled rows and many unlabelled ones. The labels steer the fit while the unlabelled rows show the shape of x. A bank holding 500 confirmed loan defaults and 50,000 unprocessed applications is in exactly this position.

Reinforcement learning has no answer column at all. An agent acts, the world returns a reward, and the agent learns which actions bring more reward over time. Nothing states the correct action for a given row; it must try and watch the result. Tuning a language model from human ratings works this way (see Unit 5).
Some syllabi group all four — supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement — under the heading "learning paradigms". The first two carry almost all of deep learning practice.

spec.aria: A number line of monthly spend with six points, dashed starting centres at 400 and 1200, the two groups coloured, and diamonds for the new centres 350 and 1250.

examples.question: A shop records six monthly spends in rupees: 300, 350, 400, 1200, 1250, 1300. (a) Each row also has a column "high spender: yes/no". Is the task supervised or unsupervised, and classification or regression? (b) Drop that column and run one round of 1-D k-means with starting centres 400 and 1200. Give the two groups and the new centres.
steps: There is an answer column, so the rows are labelled.

(a) Labelled data → supervised learning. The label takes only the values yes and no, a fixed set of classes, so the task is classification. Regression would need a numeric target, such as the exact spend next month in rupees.
(b) With the label column removed the task is unsupervised; the goal is grouping.
1-D distance is the absolute difference. Compare each spend with centre 400 and centre 1200.
examples.answer: (a) Supervised classification. (b) Group A = {300, 350, 400} with new centre ₹350; group B = {1200, 1250, 1300} with new centre ₹1250.
examples.check:
spends = [300, 350, 400, 1200, 1250, 1300]
centres = [400, 1200]
groups = [[], []]
for s in spends:
    d0 = abs(s - centres[0])
    d1 = abs(s - centres[1])
    groups[0 if d0 <= d1 else 1].append(s)
for g in groups:
    print(sum(g) / len(g))

traps: Unsupervised does not mean "no data". It means no labels. The rows are still there, usually many of them.
Cluster numbers are not classes. Cluster 1 in one run can be cluster 2 in the next, because the result depends on the starting centres.
A label stored as 0/1 is still a class when it names a category, such as spam = 1. It is regression only when the target is a real quantity where fractions make sense.
In k-means the new centre is the mean of the assigned points, not the nearest point and not the median.

quiz.q: Define supervised learning in one sentence.
quiz.a: Supervised learning fits a function f from input x to a given label y, using a set of labelled pairs (xᵢ, yᵢ).

quiz.q: State the difference between classification and regression.
quiz.a: In classification the label is a class from a fixed set; in regression the label is a real number.

quiz.q: Why can the same table serve both paradigms?
quiz.a: The feature columns x are identical either way. Adding or removing the answer column changes what we are allowed to ask, not the measured data.

quiz.q: Why must unsupervised learning invent its objective?
quiz.a: There is no y to compare against, so no error can be computed directly. We choose a goal such as tight clusters or few dimensions, then optimise that.

quiz.q: Spends 200, 240, 1000, 1100 rupees. Run one round of 1-D k-means from centres 200 and 1000. Give the groups and the new centres.
A model predicts a house price in rupees from 8 features. Supervised or unsupervised? Classification or regression? Which loss family?
quiz.a: Supervised, because labelled prices are given. Regression, because the target is a real number. Squared error is the usual loss.

quiz.q: A team clusters customers into 4 groups and names them budget, loyal, lapsed and premium. What is questionable about this?
quiz.a: Cluster numbers are not true classes and the labels can swap between runs, so the names are human interpretation. The grouping must be checked on held-out data or against business facts before the names mean anything.

quiz.q: You have 500 labelled loan defaults and 50,000 unlabelled applications. Which paradigm, and why?
quiz.a: Semi-supervised learning: train on the 500 labelled rows and let the 50,000 unlabelled rows shape the input space. Labels are expensive, and pure supervised learning on 500 rows overfits.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry most deep learning is supervised, and the real cost is labelling: annotation teams, weak labels mined from logs, and pretraining that manufactures labels from the data itself. Self-supervised learning predicts the next word or fills a masked word, so it is unsupervised in spirit but scored like supervised learning. That trick is why large language models exist at all.
